title: Listing Directory Contents
content: The ls utility lists information about files and directory contents. By default, it lists files in the current working directory in alphabetical order. Use -l for long listing format showing permissions, owner, group, file size, and timestamp. Use -a to include hidden files (files starting with a dot). Combining them as ls -la is common for comprehensive directory inspection.

title: Sorting Files by Modification Time and Size
content: ls provides sorting flags: -t sorts files by modification time (most recently modified first), -S sorts by file size (largest first), and -r reverses any sort order. Use -lh to output human-readable file sizes (K, M, G). For example, ls -lth displays the most recently updated files at the top with human-readable sizes.

title: Recursive Listing and Directory Only Display
content: Use -R to recursively list subdirectories. Use -d to list directory entries themselves rather than their contents, which is essential when globbing directories (e.g., ls -d */ lists only directories in the current folder without expanding their children). Use -1 to format output with one file per line for scripts.

title: Print Working Directory
content: pwd prints the absolute pathname of the current working directory. By default, bash's builtin pwd prints the logical directory (resolving symlinks logically with -L). Use -P to print the physical path with all symbolic links completely resolved.

title: Change Working Directory
content: cd is a shell builtin that changes the current working directory of the shell environment. Running cd with no arguments changes to the user's home directory ($HOME). Running cd .. navigates to the parent directory. Running cd - switches back to the previous working directory ($OLDPWD).

title: Physical vs Logical Directory Navigation
content: When navigating directories with symbolic links, cd -L follows logical symlinks (default behavior). cd -P forces navigation to the physical directory structure resolving all symbolic links. Quote directory paths containing spaces or special characters: cd 'my project/'.

title: Search Files by Name Pattern
content: find searches directory hierarchies in real time. Use -name followed by a quoted pattern to search filenames case-sensitively (e.g., find . -name '*.py'). Use -iname for case-insensitive filename searches (e.g., find /workspace -iname '*.log'). Always quote wildcard glob patterns to prevent premature shell expansion before find executes.

title: Filter Files by Type and Empty Status
content: Use -type to filter files by type: -type f for regular files, -type d for directories, and -type l for symbolic links. Use -empty to locate zero-byte regular files or empty directories. For example, find /workspace -type f -empty finds all blank files.

title: Search Files by Size
content: The -size option tests file sizes. Units include c (bytes), k (kilobytes), M (megabytes), G (gigabytes). A plus sign indicates greater than (+10M), a minus sign indicates less than (-1k), and no sign indicates exact size. For example, find /var/log -type f -size +50M finds log files larger than 50 megabytes.

title: Search Files by Modification and Access Time
content: -mtime matches file modification time in 24-hour days: -mtime -7 matches files modified within the last 7 days; -mtime +30 matches files older than 30 days. Use -mmin for minute granularity (e.g., -mmin -60 for files modified in the past hour). Use -atime for access time and -ctime for metadata status change time.

title: Limiting Traversal Depth
content: -maxdepth N limits directory recursion to N levels deep. -mindepth N ignores results above level N. To search only the top-level directory without entering subdirectories, use find /workspace -maxdepth 1 -type f. Combine -maxdepth 1 -mindepth 1 to inspect immediate children excluding the root argument directory itself.

title: Executing Actions on Found Files
content: -exec command {} + executes the given command with found files appended as arguments (efficient batch execution). Use {} \; to execute the command once per file. -delete deletes found files directly within find (caution: -delete implies depth-first traversal). Safety note: Always test your search criteria with -print before running destructive -exec rm or -delete.

title: Copying Files
content: cp copies files and directories. Copy a single file: cp src.txt dest.txt. Copy multiple files into a destination directory: cp f1.txt f2.txt /dest/. Use -i (interactive) to prompt before overwriting existing destination files. Use -f (force) to remove and recreate destination files if unwritable.

title: Recursive Directory Copying
content: To copy directory structures, use -r or -R (recursive). To preserve file attributes including timestamps, permissions, ownership, and symbolic links, use -a (archive mode, equivalent to -dR --preserve=all). For instance, cp -r /workspace/src /workspace/dest replicates directory contents recursively.

title: Conditional Copying and Preservation
content: -u (update) copies only when the source file is newer than the destination file or when the destination file is missing. -p preserves specified attributes (mode, ownership, timestamps). -v prints verbose descriptions of files copied.

title: Moving and Renaming Files
content: mv moves (renames) files or directories. When both arguments are files in the same filesystem, mv renames old_name.txt to new_name.txt atomically. When the final argument is a directory, mv moves all source files into that target directory.

title: Safe Overwrite Control in Moving
content: By default, mv overwrites existing destination files without prompting if permissions allow. Use -i for interactive confirmation before overwriting. Use -n (no-clobber) to prevent overwriting existing files entirely. Use -u (update) to move only when the source is newer than the destination.

title: Removing Files Safely
content: rm unlinks and removes files. rm file.txt removes the file. -i prompts before every removal. -f (force) ignores non-existent files and arguments, never prompting even if files are write-protected. Safety note: Linux has no undelete or recycle bin in the terminal; deletions with rm are permanent.

title: Recursive Directory Removal
content: To remove a non-empty directory and its entire subtree, use -r or -R (recursive). Combining with force as rm -rf removes directories and contents without prompting. Extreme caution: Avoid running rm -rf on root directories or with unchecked variable expansions (e.g., rm -rf $DIR/ when $DIR is empty).

title: Removing Empty Directories
content: rmdir removes empty directories. It fails if the directory contains any files or subdirectories, providing a built-in safety safeguard. Use -p to remove a directory and its ancestors if they become empty (e.g. rmdir -p parent/child removes child, then parent if empty).

title: Creating Directories
content: mkdir creates new directories. You can create multiple directories at once: mkdir dir1 dir2 dir3. By default, mkdir fails with an error if the directory already exists or if any parent directory along the path does not exist.

title: Creating Nested Parent Directories
content: The -p (parents) option creates intermediate parent directories as needed without reporting an error if target directories already exist. For example, mkdir -p /workspace/a/b/c creates directories a, b, and c in sequence.

title: Creating Directories with Explicit Permissions
content: Use -m (mode) to specify octal permissions during directory creation rather than relying on default umask. For example, mkdir -m 700 /workspace/private_dir creates a directory readable, writable, and searchable only by the owner.

title: Pattern Matching in Files
content: grep searches files for lines matching a specified pattern. By default, search is case-sensitive. Use -i for case-insensitive searching. For example, grep -i 'failed' /var/log/auth.log matches 'Failed', 'FAILED', and 'failed'. Always quote search patterns containing spaces or metacharacters.

title: Line Numbers and Count Output
content: -n prefixes each matching output line with its 1-based line number in the source file. -c suppresses normal output and prints only the count of matching lines. For example, grep -c 'error' debug.log outputs the total number of lines containing 'error'.

title: Inverting Matches
content: -v (invert match) selects all lines that do NOT match the specified pattern. Useful for filtering out unwanted comments, blank lines, or irrelevant categories. For example, grep -v '^#' /etc/fstab outputs configuration lines excluding comments.

title: Recursive Directory Text Search
content: -r (or -R) searches all files under each directory recursively, following symlinks if -R is used. Often combined with -n and -l: grep -rn 'DB_PASS' /workspace/config searches recursively and shows line numbers.

title: Word Boundaries and Regular Expressions
content: -w forces the pattern to match only whole words. For example, grep -w 'cat' animals.txt matches 'the cat sat' but not 'caterpillar' or 'bobcat'. Use -E for Extended Regular Expressions (ERE) allowing characters like +, ?, |, and ().

title: Listing Matching File Names
content: -l suppresses normal matching lines and prints only the names of files containing at least one match. Conversely, -L prints the names of files that do NOT contain matches. Useful in shell pipelines and file iteration.

title: Stream Editor Text Substitution
content: sed (stream editor) performs automated text transformations on standard input or files. The substitute command s/regexp/replacement/flags replaces matched patterns. Use flag g (global) to replace all occurrences on each line rather than just the first. For example, sed 's/foo/bar/g' sample.txt replaces all instances of foo with bar.

title: In-Place File Modification
content: By default, sed outputs results to standard output without altering the source file. Use -i to edit files in place. Caution: -i overwrites original file contents immediately. To create a backup copy before modification, provide an extension suffix: sed -i.bak 's/temp/final/g' document.txt.

title: Deleting Lines by Pattern or Address
content: The d command deletes lines matching an address or regex. sed '/^$/d' deletes empty lines. sed '1d' deletes the first line (useful for stripping CSV headers). sed '/pattern/d' removes all lines matching pattern.

title: Printing Specific Line Ranges
content: Use -n with the p (print) command to print only specified lines. For example, sed -n '2,4p' lines.txt prints lines 2 through 4 inclusive while suppressing all other lines. sed -n '5p' prints exactly line 5.

title: Column Extraction and Positional Fields
content: awk processes text record by record. By default, fields are delimited by contiguous whitespace. $1 represents field 1, $2 field 2, and $0 the entire record. awk '{print $1, $3}' prints fields 1 and 3 separated by an output field separator (default space).

title: Custom Field Delimiters
content: Use -F to define a custom input field separator. For example, awk -F':' '{print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd parses colon-delimited files. For CSV data, use awk -F',' '{print $2}' file.csv.

title: Conditional Filtering with Awk
content: awk allows pattern condition filters before action blocks: condition { action }. For example, awk '$3 > 100 {print $1}' prints field 1 for records where field 3 exceeds 100. awk 'length > 15' filters lines longer than 15 characters.

title: Builtin Variables: NR, NF, and END
content: awk provides built-in variables: NR is the current record number (line number); NF is the number of fields in the current record ($NF refers to the last field). The END block executes after processing all input records, useful for computing totals and averages.

title: Sorting Lines of Text
content: sort reorders lines of text alphabetically based on system locale collation. Use -r to sort in reverse (descending) order. For example, sort fruits.txt orders lines from A to Z; sort -r fruits.txt orders from Z to A.

title: Numeric Value Sorting
content: By default, sort compares character by character ('10' comes before '2'). Use -n (numeric sort) to compare by numerical value. Combine with -r as -nr for reverse numeric sorting (highest values first).

title: Sorting and Deduplicating
content: -u (unique) outputs only the first instance of lines that compare equal, eliminating duplicates during the sort operation. This is more concise and efficient than piping to uniq (sort -u file.txt).

title: Sorting by Field Key and Delimiter
content: Use -t to set a field separator and -k to define the sort key field range. For example, sort -t':' -k2,2n /workspace/passwd.txt sorts by the second colon-separated column numerically.

title: Filtering Adjacent Repeated Lines
content: uniq filters adjacent matching lines from input. Crucial requirement: uniq only detects adjacent duplicate lines; unsorted input must be sorted first (e.g., sort unsorted.txt | uniq).

title: Counting Frequency of Repeated Lines
content: -c prefixes lines by the number of occurrences. Common pipeline for frequency analysis: sort items.txt | uniq -c | sort -nr finds the most frequent items.

title: Displaying Only Duplicated or Unique Lines
content: -d outputs only duplicate lines (lines appearing 2 or more times). -u outputs only lines that appear exactly once (strictly unique). For example, uniq -d sorted.txt identifies repeated entries.

title: Counting Lines
content: wc -l counts newline characters (line count). If passed a file argument, it prints the line count and the filename. If piped via standard input or redirected (wc -l < file.txt), it outputs only the number without the filename.

title: Counting Words, Bytes, and Characters
content: -w counts words delimited by whitespace. -c counts byte length. -m counts characters (which may differ from bytes with multibyte UTF-8 characters). -L prints the length of the longest line.

title: Output Beginning of Files
content: head prints the first part of files (10 lines by default). Use -n to specify the number of lines: head -n 5 file.txt prints the first 5 lines. Use -c to print the first N bytes.

title: Output Ending of Files
content: tail prints the last part of files (10 lines by default). Use -n to specify line count: tail -n 20 app.log prints the last 20 lines. Use -n +K to start printing starting from line K through the end of the file.

title: Monitoring Growing Log Files in Real Time
content: -f (follow) causes tail to keep running and output appended data as the file grows in real time. Combine with -n to specify starting buffer: tail -n 50 -f /var/log/syslog.

title: Setting File Modes with Octal Numbers
content: chmod modifies file access permissions. Octal modes use 3 digits representing owner, group, and others: 4=read (r), 2=write (w), 1=execute (x). 755 grants rwxr-xr-x (standard executable/directory); 644 grants rw-r--r-- (standard document); 600 grants rw------- (private key/credential); 700 grants rwx------ (private directory).

title: Modifying Permissions Symbolically
content: Symbolic modes specify who (u=user/owner, g=group, o=others, a=all), an operator (+ adds, - removes, = sets), and permissions (r, w, x). For example, chmod u+x script.sh adds execute permission for owner; chmod -x locked.sh removes execution from all; chmod u+w file.txt grants write permission to user.

title: Recursive Permission Modification
content: -R modifies files and directory trees recursively. Exercise caution: chmod -R 777 grants full write permission to everyone, creating security vulnerabilities. For directory trees, prefer chmod -R 755 or use find to separate directory and file permissions.

title: Changing File Ownership and Group
content: chown changes file owner and group ownership (typically requiring administrative root privilege). Syntax: chown user:group file or chown user file. Use -R to change ownership recursively across subdirectories.

title: Creating Tape Archives
content: tar bundles multiple files and directories into a single archive file. -c creates an archive; -f specifies the archive filename. For example, tar -cf backup.tar /workspace/src packages directory src into backup.tar without compression.

title: Creating Compressed tar.gz Archives
content: -z filters the archive through gzip compression, creating .tar.gz (or .tgz) archives. Use -j for bzip2 (.tar.bz2) or -J for xz (.tar.xz). For example, tar -czf project.tar.gz /workspace/project compresses project into a compact archive.

title: Extracting Archives
content: -x extracts files from an archive. -C changes directory before extracting (e.g. tar -xzf archive.tar.gz -C /target/dir). By default, modern GNU tar automatically detects compression format when extracting with tar -xf.

title: Listing Archive Contents
content: -t lists the contents of an archive without extracting files to the filesystem. For example, tar -tf backup.tar prints all filenames stored inside backup.tar.

title: Comparing Files Line by Line
content: diff compares files line by line and outputs differences. Standard diff outputs change instructions (< lines from file1, > lines from file2). Exit code is 0 if files are identical, 1 if differences are found, and 2 if an error occurred.

title: Unified Diff Format
content: -u generates differences in unified format with surrounding context lines, preceded by + for added lines and - for deleted lines. This is the standard format used by patch files and Git diffs. diff -u v1.txt v2.txt > patch.diff saves a standard patch.

title: Directory and Brief Binary Comparison
content: -r compares subdirectories recursively. -q (brief) reports only whether files differ, suppressing detailed line differences. Combining them as diff -r -q dir1 dir2 quickly summaries differences across directories.

title: Comparing Two Sorted Files Line by Line
content: comm compares two sorted files and produces 3 columns: lines unique to file1 (col 1), unique to file2 (col 2), and common to both (col 3). Flags suppress columns: -12 prints only lines common to both files; -23 prints lines unique to file1.

title: Byte-by-Byte File Comparison
content: cmp compares two files byte by byte, making it ideal for binary files. Use -s (silent) to suppress output and check only exit code: exit code 0 indicates identical files; exit code 1 indicates differences.

title: Extracting Fields and Columns
content: cut removes sections from each line of files. -d specifies the field delimiter character; -f specifies field indexes to extract (e.g. cut -d',' -f1 data.csv extracts column 1). -f 1,3 extracts columns 1 and 3; -f 2- extracts column 2 through the end.

title: Translating and Deleting Characters
content: tr translates, squeezes, or deletes characters from standard input. tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' transforms lowercase to uppercase. -d deletes characters (e.g., tr -d '\r' removes Windows CRLF carriage returns). -s squeezes repeated characters into single occurrences.

title: Creating Empty Files and Updating Timestamps
content: touch updates file access and modification timestamps to the current time. If the target file does not exist, touch creates a new empty file. Multiple files can be created simultaneously: touch file1.txt file2.txt.

title: Displaying and Formatting Text Output
content: echo writes arguments to standard output followed by a newline. Use -n to suppress trailing newline; -e enables interpretation of backslash escapes (\n, \t). For portable, strictly formatted output, prefer printf which follows C printf syntax.

title: Concatenating and Displaying Files
content: cat reads files sequentially and writes them to standard output. Use cat file.txt to display contents. Concatenate multiple files: cat f1.txt f2.txt > combined.txt. -n adds line numbers to all output lines.

title: Shell Pipelines and Data Flow
content: A pipeline is a sequence of one or more commands separated by the pipe character '|'. The standard output (stdout, file descriptor 1) of the left command is connected via a pipe to the standard input (stdin, file descriptor 0) of the right command. In Bash, the exit status of a pipeline is the exit status of the last command unless 'set -o pipefail' is enabled.

title: Standard Output Overwrite Redirection
content: The redirection operator '>' directs the standard output of a command into a file. If the destination file exists, its contents are overwritten immediately. If it does not exist, it is created. Running > file.txt or : > file.txt truncates a file to zero bytes.

title: Standard Output Append Redirection
content: The '>>' operator appends standard output to the end of a file without overwriting existing data. If the file does not exist, it is created. Useful for continuous logging or accumulating results from loops.

title: Standard Input Redirection
content: The '<' operator causes the file to be opened on file descriptor 0 (standard input). Commands reading stdin read from the file. A key difference from passing file arguments: commands like wc -l do not output the filename when given redirected stdin.

title: Standard Error and Combined Redirection
content: File descriptor 2 represents standard error (stderr). '2> error.log' redirects errors; '2>&1' redirects stderr to wherever stdout is currently directed. Modern Bash also supports '&>' to redirect both stdout and stderr together to a file (e.g., cmd &> output.log).

title: Shell Variables and Parameter Expansion
content: Variables in Bash are assigned with VAR=value (no spaces around '='). Reference values using $VAR or ${VAR}. Use export VAR to pass variables to child processes. Special parameters include $? (exit status of last command), $# (argument count), and $$ (current process ID).

title: Quoting Mechanisms: Single vs Double Quotes
content: Single quotes ('...') preserve the literal value of every character inside; no variable expansion, command substitution, or arithmetic occurs. Double quotes ("...") preserve literal values except for '$', '`', and '\'. Always double-quote variables in command arguments (e.g., "$file") to prevent unwanted word splitting and globbing on filenames with spaces.

title: Command Substitution
content: Command substitution $(command) runs command in a subshell and replaces the syntax with its standard output, stripping trailing newlines. Prefer $(...) over the legacy backtick syntax `command`. For example, CURRENT_DATE=$(date +%Y%m%d) stores the date string into a variable.

title: Conditional Command Chaining (&& and ||)
content: Commands can be chained conditionally based on exit status: 'cmd1 && cmd2' executes cmd2 ONLY if cmd1 succeeds (exit code 0). 'cmd1 || cmd2' executes cmd2 ONLY if cmd1 fails (non-zero exit code). Semicolon ';' executes commands sequentially regardless of success.
